query_text: first satellite compared to the latest

messages.content: first satellite compared to the latest

message.content:
The **first artificial satellite** was **Sputnik 1**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**; NASA describes it as about the size of a beach ball, **58 cm** in diameter, weighing **83.6 kg**, and orbiting Earth in about **98 minutes**.[2]

If by “the latest” you mean the most recent satellites in general, they are **far larger, more complex, and far more capable** than Sputnik 1, which carried **no scientific instruments** and mainly transmitted simple radio signals.[1][2] For example, NASA notes that modern satellite missions can perform ongoing scientific work, while the early U.S. Explorer I carried a scientific payload that discovered the Van Allen radiation belts.[2]

A quick comparison:

| Feature | Sputnik 1 | Typical modern satellite |
|---|---|---|
| Launch date | 1957[2] | Ongoing, with new launches every year |
| Purpose | Proved a satellite could orbit Earth; radio beacon[1][2] | Communication, navigation, Earth observation, science, defense |
| Size / mass | 58 cm diameter; 83.6 kg[2] | Often much larger or more specialized, depending on mission |
| Instruments | None[1][2] | Often advanced sensors, computers, and payloads |
| Capability | Basic radio transmission[1][2] | High-resolution imaging, broadband links, precise timing, autonomous operations |

If you meant **“the latest satellite”** as a specific current spacecraft, tell me the mission or country and I can compare it directly with Sputnik 1.
